enrichment.short_title: Wasted costs against solicitors for misleading section 19 education JR
key_facts: A permanently excluded pupil's mother brought judicial review against the local education authority alleging breach of the section 19 duty to provide suitable education during exclusion.

Permission was granted on the papers by Mr George Bartlett QC, but the application omitted correspondence showing the child was attending CACFO full-time and that the mother had missed Coningsby PRU appointments.
The claimant sought to withdraw the claim; the LEA applied to dismiss it and for wasted costs against the claimant's solicitors, Ashok Patel.
Pitchford J held the deputy judge had been misled and that the solicitors' work fell woefully below an acceptable professional standard.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court hearing on withdrawal of a judicial review claim and the fourth defendant's application for dismissal and a wasted costs order against the claimant's solicitors.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Ashok Patel ordered to pay the fourth defendant's wasted costs on detailed assessment, including the costs of the hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Where solicitors pursue permission for judicial review on a section 19 Education Act claim while omitting material showing suitable alternative provision was available and appointments had been offered, a wasted costs order under section 51(6) of the Supreme Court Act 1981 and CPR 48.7 may be made for negligent preparation even if the conduct is not found to have been improper in the sense required for wasted costs on grounds of impropriety.
legal_issues: Whether the LEA was in breach of its section 19 duty to provide suitable education during permanent exclusion
Whether the claimant's solicitors' conduct justified a wasted costs order
Whether the solicitors intentionally misled the court on the permission application

confidence.notes: Outcome, wasted costs reasoning, and key factual omissions are clearly stated. No linked case authorities were cited in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Rent review award remitted for arbitrator's undisclosed deductions
key_facts: A rent review of commercial premises at Clayton Street West, Newcastle, for a 21-year term was referred to a surveyor arbitrator after the parties could not agree.
The arbitrator determined reviewed rent at £35,000 per annum, down from the claimant's £126,000 and above the tenant's passing rent of £27,000.

The landlord challenged the award under sections 68 and 69, complaining of undisclosed deductions for a notional rent-free period (£10,000 pa), vacant upper floors (£8,500 pa), and treatment of a £350,000 premium at 40 Collingwood Street.
Neither party had been given an opportunity to comment on those specific adjustments before the award was published.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court applications under sections 68 and 69 of the Arbitration Act 1996 to set aside or appeal a surveyor arbitrator's rent review award.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to appeal under section 69 refused; award remitted to the arbitrator for reconsideration under section 68 because of serious irregularities causing substantial injustice.
enrichment.ratio: An arbitrator who decides specific matters not raised by either party—such as a substantial notional rent-free period, a deduction for vacant upper floors, or reliance on a comparable premium without seeking clarification—commits a serious irregularity under section 68 for breach of section 33 unless the parties are given a reasonable opportunity to comment, following the principles in Zermalt Holdings and Handley v Nationwide Anglia.
legal_issues: Whether undisclosed deductions for a rent-free period and upper-floor liability constituted serious irregularity under section 68
Whether reliance on 40 Collingwood Street without clarifying the premium was a serious irregularity
Whether the arbitrator erred in law as to the tenant's repair obligations
Whether leave to appeal on a question of law should be granted under section 69
linked_authorities: Zermalt Holdings SA v Nu-Life Upholstery Repairs Ltd
Handley v Nationwide Anglia Building Society
Capital and Counties plc v Hawa
Geogas SA v Trammon Gas Ltd, The Baleares
Secretary of State for the Environment v Reed International plc

confidence.notes: Applications, irregularities identified, and remittal order are explicit. Linked authorities are cited directly in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Indecent assault convictions quashed after stepfather abuse evidence
key_facts: A R M was convicted in 1996 of two indecent assaults on sisters he babysat and sentenced to four years' imprisonment.
Leave to appeal was refused in 1997; the Criminal Cases Review Commission later investigated after the appellant saw a newspaper report.
The stepfather of the complainants had been convicted of similar offences against the same children and a third girl, over a period overlapping the alleged offences.
At trial the sisters said the appellant was the only person ever to treat them that way, but the new evidence explained their accounts and cast doubt on reliability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Further appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) following CCRC referral after earlier refused leave applications.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions quashed; defendant's costs order of £120; Crown confirmed it would not invite retrial.
enrichment.ratio: Where evidence that the complainants' stepfather committed strikingly similar offences during the same period was not before the jury, there is a real doubt that the outcome would have been the same and the convictions should be quashed.
legal_issues: Whether fresh evidence of similar offending by the stepfather undermined the safety of the 1996 convictions
Whether a retrial should be considered

confidence.notes: Outcome and reasoning are concise and clear. No statutory provisions or case citations appear in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Footpath dedication appeal dismissed over section 31 proviso
key_facts: Mr Darby owned land at Kemerton, Worcestershire, over which a disputed track was claimed as a public footpath.
Worcestershire County Council made a definitive map modification order adding the disputed path; an inspector confirmed it after a public inquiry.
The landowner argued 20 years' public use was rebutted by his 1979 diversion application, post-1979 encouragement of use, and 1986 correspondence about footpath signs.
The inspector found use as of right for 20 years and insufficient evidence of absence of intention to dedicate; the statutory appeal challenged her reasoning.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under Schedule 15 paragraph 12 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 against an inspector's decision confirming a public path order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the inspector's conclusions on section 31(1) of the Highways Act 1980 and the dedication proviso were within her fact-finding province and not Wednesbury unreasonable.
enrichment.ratio: On a statutory appeal against confirmation of a public footpath order, a landowner's application proposing that a track become a public right of way, together with later encouragement of public use, may properly be treated by the inspector as evidence of positive intention to dedicate rather than absence of intention, and the court will not substitute its own view for reasonable findings on the section 31 proviso.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector correctly applied section 31(1) of the Highways Act 1980 and the Dorset case on the dedication proviso
Whether the landowner's 1979 diversion application and 1986 correspondence showed lack of intention to dedicate
Whether the inspector's findings were unreasonable or inadequately reasoned
index_terms: R v Secretary of State ex parte Dorset County Council
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for Environment Transport and Regions ex parte Dorset County Council

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, challenged findings, and dismissal are fully set out. Dorset is the principal linked authority.

enrichment.short_title: Confiscation receiver not personally liable for defendant's CGT
key_facts: A management and enforcement receiver appointed under section 77 CJA 1988 sold assets to satisfy a £2.1 million confiscation order against Mr Piacentini after a tax fraud conviction.

The receiver sought court directions on whether she was personally assessable to capital gains tax or income tax of about £500,000 on realisations, and whether such tax was a receivership expense under section 81(5).
Lightman J held section 75 TMA 1970 did not impose personal liability because out-of-court receivers are not assessable and the section misfires for court-appointed receivers.
The defendant's continuing tax liabilities were not the receiver's expenses and could not be paid from realisations consistently with section 82(6) CJA 1988.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application by a confiscation enforcement receiver for directions on personal tax liability and whether tax is payable as a receivership expense.
enrichment.outcome: Receiver held not assessable to capital gains tax or income tax; defendant's tax liabilities are not an expense of the receivership within section 81(5) or section 88(2) of the CJA 1988.
enrichment.ratio: A receiver appointed under the Criminal Justice Act 1988 to realise a convicted offender's property is not personally assessable under sections 75 and 77 of the Taxes Management Act 1970, and the offender's capital gains and income tax liabilities on realisation are not receiver's expenses payable from confiscation proceeds because section 81 sets out an exhaustive scheme and section 82(6) excludes conflicting obligations of the defendant.
legal_issues: Whether a CJA receiver is personally assessable to CGT and income tax under sections 75 and 77 TMA 1970
Whether the defendant's tax on realisations is an expense of the receivership under section 81(5) CJA 1988
How Mesco Properties applies to the order of application of realisation proceeds
linked_authorities: Hughes v Commissioners of Customs & Excise
In Re Beni Felkai Mining Company Ltd
Radford and Hayward v Northavon RDC

confidence.notes: Both issues for directions and holdings are clearly reasoned with extensive statutory and case analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Legal advice privilege covers BIU contact with former Bank officers
key_facts: This addendum judgment followed an earlier ruling on legal professional privilege in litigation arising from the Bingham Inquiry into BCCI supervision.
The Bank's Bingham Inquiry Unit consulted former senior officers including Lord Richardson and Peter Cooke about knowledge acquired during their Bank service.
Claimants argued former officers were third parties so communications were not privileged.
Tomlinson J held former officers who acquired confidential Bank knowledge in their official capacity were part of the Bank's team for privilege purposes, not external consultants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Addendum High Court ruling on legal professional privilege following a December 2002 judgment in the Three Rivers litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Communications between the BIU and former Bank officers concerned with BCCI supervision are protected by legal advice privilege where the dominant purpose test is satisfied; common interest privilege not decided.
enrichment.ratio: Where a corporation gathers from former officers information that was known to the corporation through those officers in their official capacity, communications for the dominant purpose of obtaining legal advice are protected by legal advice privilege; former officers are not third parties analogous to external experts in Wheeler v Le Marchant.
legal_issues: Whether communications with former Bank officers are protected by legal advice privilege
Whether former officers should be treated as third parties outside the client team
Whether common interest privilege alternatively applies

confidence.notes: Short addendum with clear ratio on former officers and privilege. No statutes cited; linked cases referenced in judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Part 36 indemnity costs after beating own vintage car offer
key_facts: Mrs Neave and her son disputed ownership of nine historic vehicles after he removed five from her property in 1998.
At trial she recovered six vehicles and £3,000 trespass damages; the judge ordered the son to pay one-third of her costs on the standard basis.
She had made Part 36 offers in April and July 2001 proposing return of five specified vehicles plus costs; the defendant ignored them.
The costs judge did not address CPR 36.21 despite written submissions; the Court of Appeal held the judgment beat the Part 36 offer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission limited to whether the judge should have made an order under CPR 36.21 after the claimant beat her own Part 36 offer at trial.
enrichment.outcome: Costs appeal allowed; indemnity costs from 17 May 2001 ordered with interest; prior standard-basis costs order before that date undisturbed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant's Part 36 offer is valid—technical defects being curable under CPR 36.1(2)—and the trial judgment is more advantageous than the offer, CPR 36.21 requires indemnity costs unless unjust; a judge who fails to consider rule 36.21 after the point was raised has not properly exercised the costs discretion.
legal_issues: Whether the April and July 2001 letters were valid Part 36 offers
Whether the trial judgment was more advantageous to the claimant than the Part 36 proposals
Whether it would be unjust to order indemnity costs under CPR 36.21(4)
linked_authorities: Eagil Trust Co Ltd v Pigott-Brown
Mannai Investment Co Ltd v Eagle Star Life Assurance Co Ltd

confidence.notes: Permission was limited to CPR 36.21; substantive ownership appeal was refused. Part 36 analysis and outcome are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Arbitrator's local market knowledge not section 68 irregularity
key_facts: Checkpoint Ltd challenged a rent review award fixing rent at £440,000 for Arrow Point, Bracknell, double the 1995 rent.
The surveyor arbitrator preferred Winnersh Triangle comparables over Unit 3 Doncastle Road and drew on his personal letting experience at Winnersh Triangle.
The tenant argued this was fresh evidence and a failure to deal with over-supply and poor demand in Bracknell.
Park J rejected the challenge; the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on both grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from a High Court refusal to set aside a rent review award for serious irregularity under section 68 of the Arbitration Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no serious irregularity in the arbitrator using personal market knowledge to evaluate evidence or in failing to deal separately with over-supply submissions.
enrichment.ratio: An expert arbitrator may rely on personal knowledge fairly used to evaluate competing evidence on comparability and market demand where the point was central to the parties' submissions and within the expertise the lease required; such use is not fresh evidence or inquisitorial procedure, and subservient arguments about over-supply need not be resolved separately under section 68(2)(d).
legal_issues: Whether the arbitrator committed serious irregularity by relying on personal experience of Winnersh Triangle lettings without disclosure
Whether use of personal knowledge breached agreed inquisitorial procedure directions
Whether failure to address over-supply and poor demand evidence was failure to deal with an issue under section 68(2)(d)
Whether any irregularity caused substantial injustice
index_terms: Egmatra AG v Marco Trading Corporation
linked_authorities: Top Shop Estates Ltd v Danino
Winchester City Council v Secretary of State for the Environment
Egmatra AG v Marco Trading Corporation
English v Emery Reimbold & Strick Ltd
Egil Trust Co Ltd v Pigott-Brown

enrichment.short_title: Sea lice pyrethroid patent invalid for anticipation and obviousness
key_facts: Vericore appealed invalidation of UK patent GB 2,270,261 for using pyrethroid pesticides to treat sea lice on salmon in seawater.
The Comptroller held claims 1 and 4 anticipated by prior Norwegian research (D2, D9) using pyrethrum and all claims obvious over Dr Horsberg's thesis (D1) and related art.
The patentee argued pyrethroid meant synthetic compounds only and prior kill rates below 95% were not treatment within the claims.
Laddie J dismissed the appeal, finding pyrethroid includes natural pyrethrins and prior art disclosed effective treatment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Patents Court appeal on a rehearing from the Comptroller's decision revoking the patent for lack of novelty and obviousness.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; patent invalid for anticipation over D2 and D9 and obviousness over D1, with claims 6, 8 and 9 also obvious.
enrichment.ratio: In the fish health field at the priority date, pyrethroid commonly included natural pyrethrins as well as synthetics, so prior use of pyrethrum to delouse salmon anticipated a claim to pyrethroid treatment; where D1 pointed to synthetic pyrethroids as the probable way forward after promising pyrethrum trials, the skilled team would obviously try them, including as a water suspension.
legal_issues: Whether pyrethroid in the claims excludes natural pyrethrins and pyrethrum
Whether D2 and D9 anticipate for lack of sufficient efficacy to constitute treatment
Whether D1 was published prior art before the priority date
Who is the skilled addressee for obviousness
Whether suspension claims 6, 8 and 9 involve an inventive step

confidence.notes: Novelty and obviousness holdings are detailed with prior art documents D1, D2 and D9. Patents Act 1977 is the governing statute though not quoted by section.

enrichment.short_title: Defamation offer of amends compensation for Cleese article
key_facts: John Cleese complained of an Evening Standard article of 11 April 2002 suggesting he faced humiliation after a US TV flop and that America had turned on him.
Associated Newspapers made an accepted offer of amends under the Defamation Act 1996; parties could not agree compensation or apology terms.
The article misstated Cleese's role in the cancelled series, his US reputation, and attributed quotations he denied making.
A correction was published on 23 July 2002 with less prominence than the original; Eady J assessed compensation at £13,500.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Assessment of compensation under section 3(5) of the Defamation Act 1996 following acceptance of a statutory offer of amends without commenced proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Compensation assessed at £13,500 on the same principles as libel damages, taking account of the published apology and mitigation steps.
enrichment.ratio: Compensation under section 3(5) of the Defamation Act 1996 is determined on the same principles as defamation damages, including gravity, publication scale, hurt feelings and vindication, with adjustment for steps taken in fulfilment of the offer; the procedure is not summary or capped and requires a full evaluative hearing, not rough-and-ready assessment.
legal_issues: The appropriate level of compensation under section 3(5) Defamation Act 1996
How far the published apology and delay mitigate compensation
Whether without-prejudice negotiation figures should influence judicial assessment
Procedural guidance for resolving offer of amends disputes
linked_authorities: Lillie and Reed v Newcastle City Council

confidence.notes: Detailed judgment on offer of amends procedure and specific compensation figure. Defamatory meanings and mitigation are fully analysed.
